title: KVMSR+UDWeave: Extreme-Scaling with Fine-grained Parallelism on the UpDown Graph Supercomputer
problem: Irregular graph applications are challenging to program on scalable supercomputers. Achieving extreme-scale performance (million-fold parallelism) on skewed graphs requires new programming models and abstractions.
motivation: Graph algorithms are critical for intelligence and national security (IARPA AGILE program) but notoriously difficult to scale. Fine-grained parallelism and proper data placement are essential but hard to express with traditional models.
method: KVMSR+UDWeave works by separating three programming decisions that are usually tangled together: how many tasks run in parallel, which processor handles which task, and where data gets stored. The UpDown supercomputer makes this possible through two built-in features: you can name specific processor locations for computations to run on, and every processor can see the same addresses in memory (shared global address space). This separation allows programmers to write code that takes full advantage of the hardware's parallelism, even for irregular graph algorithms where some parts have far more work than others.
key_novelty: The innovation is separating how many things run in parallel from where they run and where their data lives, which unlocks extreme-scale performance for irregular graph algorithms on the UpDown supercomputer.
contributions: KVMSR+UDWeave programming model for graph algorithms
Clean separation of parallelism, binding, and data placement
Reduced programming effort for scalable graph algorithms
Multiple graph benchmarks and workflows in IARPA AGILE program
Excellent strong-scaling to million-fold hardware parallelism
High absolute performance on real-world skewed graphs
limitations: Specific to UpDown architecture; simulation-based results; irregular workloads inherently harder to scale; skewed graph distribution challenges.
